issues.legal_issue: A spouse’s patently false, reckless and defamatory accusations against the other spouse may constitute mental cruelty warranting divorce, whereas filing a complaint alone, or the absence of action or an acquittal following a complaint, does not by itself establish cruelty.
material_facts: The wife made serious allegations of abuse and other misconduct against the husband and his relatives in newspaper reports and complaints to several authorities.
Police investigations found the allegations baseless and false; in a later complaint, the police also found that the wife’s injuries were self-inflicted.
The police findings had attained finality, proceedings had been initiated against the wife in relation to a false complaint, and no criminal case remained pending against the husband.
The husband relied on the complaints and accusations as cruelty in his divorce petition.
issues.conclusion: The wife’s patently false and defamatory accusations amounted to mental cruelty, and the husband was entitled to a decree of divorce.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, cruelty is assessed in light of the entire facts and circumstances and has no exact or closed definition. As stated in K. Srinivas Rao v. D.A. Deepa, relying on the illustrative instances in Samar Ghosh v. Jaya Ghosh, unfounded indecent defamatory allegations and repeated false complaints may, in the facts of a case, cause mental cruelty. Ravi Kumar v. Julmidevi likewise explains that cruelty in matrimonial relationships is context-dependent and may take varied forms. Mere filing of a complaint is not cruelty where there are justifiable grounds; nor does the mere absence of action on a complaint or an acquittal establish cruelty. Patently false allegations, however, may constitute cruelty.

rule.if: divorce_proceeding and accusations_made_against_spouse and accusations_found_patently_false and accusations_defamatory

predicates.divorce_proceeding: A spouse sought dissolution of the marriage on the ground of the other spouse’s conduct.
predicates.accusations_made_against_spouse: One spouse made accusations of misconduct against the other spouse.
predicates.accusations_found_patently_false: The accusations were found to be patently false on the evidence or investigation relied on by the court.
predicates.accusations_defamatory: The accusations were of a kind that could lower the other spouse’s reputation.

issues.definition: When a spouse seeks divorce based on accusations by the other spouse, and those accusations are found patently false and are defamatory, the rule treats them as mental cruelty.

issues.legal_issue: When granting a divorce, the court may make a permanent financial and residential arrangement for a spouse whose housing needs require continuing provision.
material_facts: The wife continued to live in a house owned by the husband’s mother, while the husband lived separately with his parents.
The parties’ son and daughter-in-law lived with the wife, but the court considered that they might not continue to live with her indefinitely.
The court noted the parties’ status and that the husband was paying maintenance to the wife.
The court ordered permanent alimony and directed that the wife could remain in her current residence until a suitable flat was provided in her name.
issues.conclusion: The wife was awarded one-time permanent alimony and a residential flat; she could continue living in her current residence until the flat was provided.
issues.legal_principle: In making the final matrimonial disposition, the Court considered the wife’s need for a decent and lasting residence, the possibility that her son and daughter-in-law might not continue living with her, and the parties’ status. The judgment cited no separate statutory provision or earlier case for this arrangement.

rule.if: divorce_proceeding and divorce_granted and spouse_needs_continuing_housing and current_housing_is_not_a_permanent_arrangement

predicates.divorce_proceeding: A court considered a proceeding seeking dissolution of a marriage.
predicates.spouse_needs_continuing_housing: The court found that a spouse required a lasting residential arrangement.
predicates.current_housing_is_not_a_permanent_arran: The spouse’s existing housing depended on a living arrangement that might not continue indefinitely.

issues.definition: When a divorce is granted and a spouse needs lasting housing but the existing arrangement may not continue, the rule provides for permanent financial and residential support.
